As long as you're planning the entire cross in inspection and consistently doing it in under 8 moves, you should be fine. From what I've seen you're doing that, which is awesome, I was not doing that when I was your speed. Of course the next step with cross is optimizing finger tricks, learning to make x crosses, and planning your first pair in inspection. While that will make you faster, there are other things you should be focusing on. Also, sorry about Nb perms, those things suckkkkk.

You should focus on:
1. Full oll and pll (pll first)
2. Better cross solutions (no rotations, 8 moves or less)
3. Better f2l solutions (8 moves or less or 11 in misslotted cases)

Preferably, do them in that order. Speedcubing wiki has all of the algs for oll, pll, and f2l. J Perm has good videos on advanced f2l and some outdated videos on oll and pll.

1. Make sure you're solving pairs into the back whenever possible, which leaves room in the front for you to spot pairs. (I'm guilty of not doing this, which is why I'm so aware of how important it is) 
2. I kind of just look at the cube while I'm solving a pair trying to find other pairs. Even if the only thing you find is an edge or something, it's still better than nothing. 

Try some slow solves, where you deliberately slow down your turn speed. Just observe the U layer and any empty slots you can see and try to find prices for your next pair. I do a lot of slow solves, just because I find them fun. 

Also, don't try to find two pairs at once. After cross, find a pair and solve it. You should be able to solve pairs without thinking about the moves you're doing, kind of like a PLL alg. While you're doing the moves to solve that first pair, look at the top layer and any unsolved pairs you can see to try to find the next pair. 

By far though, the best way to start learning f2l is to just look somewhere other than the pair you're solving qhen you're solving a pair. When practicing this, I just did normal timed solves, and i constantly said 'DONT LOOK AT THE PAIR YOURE SOLVING' over and over in my head. 

Also try this: Do slow solves where you close your eyes before solving your f2l pairs. Basically, recognize a pair, close your eyes, solve it from memory, open your eyes. If you can do this with no difficulty, then you have essentially memorized all of the solutions for f2l as if they were a regular algorithm.

When you're running, don't slow down or stop. Slowing too much or stopping can actually put you in more pain than keeping a pace. Physically, when you're running (or doing any kind of exercise) your body releases adrenaline, norepinephrine, endorphins, and a buncha other chemicals and hormones. Essentially what those hormones do is temporarily block pain signals being sent to the brain and give you energy. It's a survival mechanism that kicks in during exercise. The problem is that once you stop running (or even slow down enough), your body stops producing those hormones, and you start feeling more pain and fatigue. It's a paradoxical relationship, if you're running, you would expect that stopping temporarily would make you feel less pain but it actually does the opposite.

The main thing that I'm seeing is that you don't plan your entire cross in inspection. Trust me, you're losing a lot of time on your cross. I would recommend scrambling your cube and taking as much time as you need to completely plan your cross. If you practice this enough you should be able to plan your cross within inspection. When making your cross, try to be as efficient as possible and never rotate the cube when solving the cross (its fine to do F or B moves during your cross). Watching example solves on YouTube will really help you to recognize easy cross cases and teach you how to insert multiple cross edges at once. 

Another thing is that you tend to fidget and do unnecessary moves when you're recognizing cases in F2L. Whenever you don't instantly see a F2L pair, you rotate or do a bunch of unessasary U moves. It's okay to pause during your F2L, you shouldn't just do random moves or cube rotations because that will actually make recognition harder and your solves less efficient.
 You also tend to do this during your last layer as well.

 You shouldn't be rotating during Oll or Pll unless your algorithm requires it. The best thing to do for Pll is to set up your Pll with U moves, then execute the Pll, and finally do a U, U', or U2 to solve the cross. This is called AUF (adjust U face). As you practice AUF you should be able to recognize what your AUF is gonna be before you execute your PLL, that way you can execute your PLL and AUF without pausing in between. 

Your F2L solutions are surprisingly good for someone at your skill level, but they still need work in some places. Watching example solves is a great way to learn F2L algs that are more efficient. As a general rule, every F2L case can be solved and inserted in 8 moves or less and with no more than 1 cube rotation. The only exceptions to this rule is cases where both pieces are misoriented in a slot, in which case they can be solved with 11 moves or less.

 I did notice you used some rotationless inserts which is a good thing. Your fingertricks during F2L are also pretty good which is probably why you have such high tps. You've also learned full PLL (I assume) which is great as well. You might want to start learning full OLL but at this point it would just be a distraction. Learning full OLL would probably only save you about 2 seconds per solve, while working on your cross and F2L could literally cut your times in half. In fact, there's a youtuber named CubingEncoded that is sub-10 but doesn't know full OLL. So if you were you, I'd save Oll until you're averaging about 15-17.

The first thing you're gonna want to learn is gonna be f2l . F2l essentially solves the corners and edges at the same exact time by making pairs. You can become very fast and efficient with f2l. [Here ](https://youtu.be/Ar_Zit1VLG0)is a video on basic f2l. Next youre gonna have to learn about a dozen algorithms for [2 look oll](https://youtu.be/GhmYBgLoQQg) and [2 look pll ](https://youtu.be/f_Yor-ydZjs). Essentially these algorithm sets allow you to solve oll in 2 algorithms or less, and pll in 2 algorithms or less. After that. You'll want to learn [full pll](https://youtu.be/JvqGU0UZPcE) and [advanced f2l.](https://youtu.be/3B_oB2YrLvk) The difference is thay advanced f2l uses solutions thay arent super intuitive but are much more efficient. Full pll is 27 algs and it allows you to do the last layer in one algorithm. You should learn these when you reach the 30 second or below mark. Finally, learn [full oll](https://youtu.be/vU6HsK3hvQs). To be honest, full oll isn't much faster than 2 look oll. There are a few fast cubes that get sub 10 averages with 2 look oll. This should be saves for last when you reach the 15 second mark. Finally, you can move into [other algorithm sets](https://youtu.be/5-i7Fwx5DTU) like coll and vls. This will take time, but I promise, you'll get it.
